# Object Detection {.unnumbered}

![](images/jpeg/cover.jpg){width=70% fig-align="center"}

## Overview {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-overview-1193}

The [Image Classification](../image_classification/image_classification.qmd) lab trained a classifier and deployed it to the Arduino UNO Q, first on static images and then on a live camera feed, with the result driving the LED matrix over Bridge. This lab takes the next step in computer vision: **object detection**.

A classifier answers one question about the whole image: *what is this?* A detector answers two questions for every object it finds: *what is it, and where is it?* That second answer is what makes counting, tracking, sorting, and spatial reasoning possible.

This lab has two parts:

- **Part 1** runs the UNO Q's pre-installed object detection examples. The first is a **static image detector**: a photo uploaded through a web browser comes back with bounding boxes drawn on it. The second runs the same model on a **live camera feed**.
- **Part 2** builds a **custom object detector** with Edge Impulse Studio, trained to find **boxes** and **wheels** on a workbench, and deploys it to the UNO Q with App Lab Bricks, first for static images and then for live webcam inference.

As before, the lab uses the UNO Q's dual-brain architecture: **Python on the MPU** for AI inference and an **Arduino sketch on the MCU** for physical feedback. This time the MCU does not just show a label. It shows a **count** of each object type on the LED matrix, updated as objects enter and leave the camera's view.

### Learning Objectives {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-learning-objectives-2798}

- Understand how object detection differs from image classification, and how detectors are evaluated (IoU, mAP).
- Run the pre-installed Object Detection and Video Object Detection Bricks.
- Label a bounding-box dataset and train **FOMO** and **YOLO** models in Edge Impulse Studio.
- Deploy a custom detector through **App Lab Bricks**, on static images and on a live camera feed.
- Turn detections into **counts** and send them to the MCU over Bridge RPC.
- Handle the "nothing detected" case in a live detection app.

## From Image Classification to Object Detection {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-image-classification-object-detection-82f8}

Object detection builds on image classification but extends it in an important way:

- **Image classification** assigns a single label to the entire image and answers: "What is the main object or scene in this image?"
- **Object detection** identifies and locates multiple objects in an image and answers: "Which objects are in this image, and where is each one?" Its output is a list of predictions, each with a **class label**, a **confidence score**, and a **location**.

\noindent
![](images/jpeg/objxclas.jpg){width=85% fig-align="center"}

A detector therefore combines two tasks:

1. **Localization**: finding where each object is, usually as a rectangular **bounding box**.
2. **Classification**: deciding what each localized object is, exactly as a classifier would, but per region.

This makes detection harder than classification. An image can contain several objects of different classes, at different sizes, partially hidden behind each other, against a cluttered background, and an edge application usually needs all of that in real time.

### Single-Stage Detectors {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-singlestage-detectors-a3e7}

Early detectors worked in two stages: first propose regions that might contain an object, then classify each region (R-CNN and its descendants). They are accurate but too slow for an edge device.

Every model in this lab is a **single-stage detector**, which predicts locations and classes in one forward pass through the network:

- **YOLO** (You Only Look Once) divides the image into a grid and predicts boxes and classes for every cell at once. It is the family behind the UNO Q's pre-installed model (YOLOX).
- **SSD MobileNet** pairs a MobileNet backbone with a Single Shot Detector head.
- **FOMO** (Faster Objects, More Objects), developed by Edge Impulse, drops the bounding box entirely and predicts only each object's **centroid**. @sec-uno-q-object-detection-fomo-works-9cea looks at it in more detail.

### How Detectors Are Evaluated {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-detectors-evaluated-3394}

Accuracy alone does not describe a detector, because a prediction can have the right class in the wrong place. Three measures matter:

- **Intersection over Union (IoU)** measures how well a predicted box overlaps the ground-truth box drawn by a human: the area of their intersection divided by the area of their union. An IoU of 1.0 is a perfect match. A detection usually counts as correct when IoU ≥ 0.5.

\noindent
![](images/png/iou.png){width=70% fig-align="center"}

- **Mean Average Precision (mAP)** combines classification and localization into one number. For each class, precision is averaged across recall levels, and the result is averaged across classes. "mAP@0.5" means a detection counts as correct when its IoU is at least 0.5. Edge Impulse reports mAP for YOLO and SSD models.

\noindent
![](images/png/map.png){width=70% fig-align="center"}

- **Frames per second (FPS)**, or its inverse, latency per frame. At the edge, a model that is 3% more accurate but three times slower is often the wrong choice.

### Overlapping Detections and NMS {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-overlapping-detections-nms-389e}

A detector often reports the same object several times, with slightly different boxes and confidences. **Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)** cleans this up: keep the most confident box, discard every other box of the same class that overlaps it beyond an IoU threshold, and repeat. On the UNO Q, NMS is not something to implement: the Edge Impulse model file (`.eim`) already includes it, so the Bricks receive the final, de-duplicated list.

### From the Raspberry Pi to the UNO Q {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-raspberry-pi-uno-q-474e}

The [Raspberry Pi Object Detection](../../../raspi/object_detection/object_detection.qmd) lab, and the object detection chapters of [EdgeML Made Easy](https://mjrovai.github.io/EdgeML_Made_Ease_ebook/), train this same box-and-wheel detector and run it on a Raspberry Pi. The UNO Q approach differs as follows:

+--------------------------+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| **Aspect**               | **Raspberry Pi (Zero 2 W / 5)**  | **Arduino UNO Q**                 |
+:=========================+:=================================+:==================================+
| **Camera**               | CSI camera or USB webcam         | USB webcam (or CSI via the Media  |
|                          |                                  | Carrier)                          |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| **Model format**         | `.tflite` (LiteRT) or `.eim`     | `.eim`, loaded by an App Lab      |
|                          |                                  | Brick                             |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| **Inference code**       | Custom Python: preprocessing,    | A Brick call: `detect()` or a     |
|                          | tensors, NMS, drawing            | callback                          |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| **Live stream to the     | A custom Flask app               | Built into the Video Object       |
| browser**                |                                  | Detection Brick                   |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| **Physical output**      | GPIO from Python (no real-time   | Dedicated MCU via Bridge RPC      |
|                          | guarantees)                      |                                   |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| **Deployment**           | Run a Python script              | Package model, Python, and sketch |
|                          |                                  | as one App                        |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+

: Object detection on the Raspberry Pi and the UNO Q. {#tbl-uno-q-object-detection-raspi-vs-uno-q}

On the Pi, the whole inference pipeline is written by hand, which is the best way to understand it. On the UNO Q, the Bricks hide that pipeline, so the work moves to what the application **does** with the detections.

> A `.tflite` (LiteRT) model also runs on the UNO Q, the same way as on the Raspberry Pi.

## Part 1: The Pre-Installed Object Detectors {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-part-1-preinstalled-object-detectors-3711}

The UNO Q ships with a general-purpose detector: a **YOLOX-Nano** model trained on the [COCO dataset](https://cocodataset.org), which recognizes 80 everyday classes such as person, cup, cell phone, bottle, chair, cat, and dog. Two examples use it.

+------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+---------------------------+
| **Example**                  | **Bricks**                              | **Input**                 |
+:=============================+:========================================+:==========================+
| **Detect objects on images** | `object_detection` and `web_ui`         | Static image uploaded in  |
|                              |                                         | the browser               |
+------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+---------------------------+
| **Detect Objects on Camera** | `video_object_detection` and `web_ui`   | Live USB webcam           |
+------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+---------------------------+

: The pre-installed object detection examples. {#tbl-uno-q-object-detection-examples}

First, confirm the exact App IDs on the board, since they can change between App Lab releases:

```bash
arduino-app-cli app list --examples | grep -i detect
```

\noindent
![](images/png/list-examples-detect.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

The two used here are `examples:inspirational/object-detection` (**Detect objects on images**) and `examples:inspirational/video-generic-object-detection` (**Detect Objects on Camera**). The list also shows short, single-purpose examples for each Brick, under `examples:bricks/arduino/object_detection/...` and `examples:bricks/arduino/video_object_detection/...`. One of them, `02_count_objects`, counts detections per label, which is the starting point for @sec-uno-q-object-detection-postprocessing-counting-mcu-actuation-via-bridge-d4a5.

### The Architecture {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-architecture-6c18}

The static image example works exactly like the image classification example, with one difference: the board sends back an **image** with the boxes drawn on it, not just a list of labels.

```text
Browser (your PC)                          UNO Q (MPU / Python)
+-------------------+                     +-------------------------+
|                   |   Upload image      |                         |
|  Web UI (port     | ------------------> |  ObjectDetection Brick  |
|  7000)            |   (base64 via       |  (YOLOX-Nano, COCO)     |
|                   |    WebSocket)       |                         |
|  Shows annotated  | <------------------ |  draw_bounding_boxes()  |
|  image + count    |   PNG with boxes    |  -> base64 PNG          |
+-------------------+                     +-------------------------+
```

### Step 1: Start the Static Image Example {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-1-start-static-image-example-cbcc}

> **This step does not need a webcam.**

```bash
arduino-app-cli app start examples:inspirational/object-detection
```

\noindent
![](images/png/objdet-start.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

### Step 2: Open the Web UI and Detect {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-2-open-web-ui-detect-649c}

On the host computer, open `http://<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:7000`. Upload a photo with several everyday objects in it (a desk with a cup, a phone, and a bottle works well), set the **confidence threshold** slider, and click **Run detection**.

\noindent
![](images/png/ban-apple.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

Try the same image at different thresholds. At a high threshold (0.7), only the objects the model is sure about appear. At a low one (0.2), more objects appear, along with false positives. That slider is the single most important tuning knob in any detection application, and Part 2 returns to it.

> As with the classification example, the results go to the browser over WebSocket, not to the terminal log.

### Step 3: Study the Source Code {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-3-study-source-code-15be}

```bash
cat /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
object-detection/python/main.py
```

> **Where the examples live.** The App ID `examples:inspirational/object-detection` maps to the folder `/var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/object-detection`. The `common/` level holds examples that run on every board, and board-specific ones sit next to it, such as `platform_unoq/`. If a path in this lab does not exist on the board, find it with `sudo find /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples -type d -name "object-detection"`.

The core of it, in a simplified excerpt:

```python
from arduino.app_utils import *
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.object_detection import ObjectDetection

object_detection = ObjectDetection()

def on_detect_objects(client_id, data):
    image_bytes = base64.b64decode(data.get('image'))
    pil_image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(image_bytes))
    confidence = data.get('confidence', 0.5)

    results = object_detection.detect(pil_image,
                                      confidence=confidence)
    img_with_boxes = object_detection.draw_bounding_boxes(
        pil_image, results)
    # ... encode img_with_boxes as a base64 PNG into `response` ...
    ui.send_message('detection_result', response)

ui = WebUI()
ui.on_message('detect_objects', on_detect_objects)
App.run()
```

Compared to the classification example:

- `ObjectDetection()` replaces `ImageClassification()`, and `detect()` replaces `classify()`.
- `draw_bounding_boxes()` is new. The Brick draws the boxes and labels, so the application never handles pixel coordinates unless it needs to.
- The structure is otherwise identical: event-driven, no `user_loop`, no Bridge, no MCU.

The result of `detect()` is a dictionary with a single key, `detection`, holding one entry per object found:

```python
{
  "detection": [
    {"class_name": "cup", "confidence": "87.50",
     "bounding_box_xyxy": [41.0, 112.0, 98.0, 180.0]},
    {"class_name": "cell phone", "confidence": "64.12",
     "bounding_box_xyxy": [150.0, 60.0, 210.0, 170.0]}
  ]
}
```

The values above are illustrative, but the format is exact. Two details matter:

- `bounding_box_xyxy` is `[x1, y1, x2, y2]`: the top-left and bottom-right corners, in pixels.
- `confidence` in the **result** is a **string**, formatted as a percentage from 0 to 100 (`"87.50"`). The `confidence` **parameter** passed to `detect()` is a **float** from 0.0 to 1.0. Mixing the two scales is an easy mistake, so convert with `float(obj["confidence"]) / 100` before comparing.

Stop the example when done:

```bash
arduino-app-cli app stop examples:inspirational/object-detection
```

\noindent
![](images/png/stop-app.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

### Step 4: Run the Live Camera Example {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-4-run-live-camera-example-6b79}

Connect the webcam through the powered hub and start the second example:

```bash
arduino-app-cli app start \
  examples:inspirational/video-generic-object-detection
```

Open `http://<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:7000` again. This time the page shows the **live camera feed with bounding boxes drawn in real time**, each labeled with its class and confidence. On the right are a **Confidence** slider, a **Feedback** panel, and a running list of **Recent detections** with their confidence and timestamp. Point the camera at a cup, a phone, or a person.

\noindent
![](images/png/video-objdet-example.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

The **Feedback** panel is the example's "special reaction": when one of a handful of COCO classes appears (cat, cell phone, clock, cup, dog, or potted plant), it shows a short message for that object. Here, a cup on the desk triggered "Need a break?". Note also that the confidence slider is set to 0.51, and the cup is detected at only 0.55–0.57: raise the threshold slightly and the cup disappears, while the keyboard (0.87–0.89) stays. That is the threshold trade-off from Step 2, now happening live.

The architecture has one extra piece:

```text
USB webcam -> VideoObjectDetection Brick -> model runner (YOLOX-Nano)
                                             |                \
                                 detections (WebSocket)   annotated video
                                             |           (port 4912, /embed)
                                on_detect_all(callback)          |
                                             |                   |
                               ui.send_message("detection")      |
                                             \                  /
                                              Browser (port 7000)
```

The video with boxes is produced by the **model runner** itself and served on port **4912**; the web page simply embeds `http://<UNO_Q_IP>:4912/embed` in an `iframe`. The Python code never touches a frame. It only receives the detections, through callbacks. The source:

```bash
cat /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
video-generic-object-detection/python/main.py
```

```python
from arduino.app_utils import App
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.video_objectdetection import (
    VideoObjectDetection,
)
from datetime import datetime, UTC

ui = WebUI()
detection_stream = VideoObjectDetection(confidence=0.5,
                                        debounce_sec=0.0)

ui.on_message(
    "override_th",
    lambda sid, threshold: detection_stream.override_threshold(threshold),
)

def send_detections_to_ui(detections: dict):
  for key, values in detections.items():
    for value in values:
      entry = {
        "content": key,
        "confidence": value.get("confidence"),
        "timestamp": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()
      }
      ui.send_message("detection", message=entry)

detection_stream.on_detect_all(send_detections_to_ui)

App.run()
```

Note the shape of `detections`. It is **grouped by label**, with a list of every instance of that label in the frame:

```python
{
  "cup":    [{"confidence": 0.91, "bounding_box_xyxy": (41, 112, 98, 180)}],
  "person": [{"confidence": 0.88, "bounding_box_xyxy": (...)},
             {"confidence": 0.62, "bounding_box_xyxy": (...)}]
}
```

That grouping makes counting trivial: `len(detections["person"])` is the number of people in the frame. Note also that here `confidence` is a **float from 0 to 1**, unlike the static Brick's percentage string.

The slider calls `override_threshold()`, which changes the threshold inside the running model without restarting the app.

Stop the example:

```bash
arduino-app-cli app stop \
  examples:inspirational/video-generic-object-detection
```

### Running the Examples from Arduino App Lab {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-running-examples-arduino-app-lab-8418}

As with image classification, both examples are also available in App Lab on the host computer: connect to the UNO Q over Wi-Fi, open **Inspirations**, and choose **Detect objects on images** or **Detect Objects on Camera**. The camera example must run in **Network Mode**, because the webcam occupies the hub. While an app runs, its card shows **Running**, and the bottom bar shows its name with a **Stop** button.

\noindent
![](images/png/applab-objdet-examples.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

Two more Inspirations use the same detector and are worth a look:

- **Detect Objects on Smartphone Camera** runs the same live detection on a phone's camera instead of a USB webcam. Without a webcam or a powered hub, this is a way to try live detection right away.
- **Object Hunting** turns detection into a game: the app gives a list of objects to find and show to the camera.

### What Part 1 Shows {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-part-1-shows-8bba}

The pre-installed detector is impressive, but it has the same limitations the classification example had:

- It knows only COCO's 80 classes and has never seen the objects of a specific project.
- Results stay in the browser. Nothing physical happens.
- YOLOX-Nano is sized for general use, not for the speed a given application might need.

Part 2 trains a model on custom objects, deploys it with the same two Bricks, and connects it to the MCU.

## Part 2: Building a Custom Object Detector {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-part-2-building-custom-object-detector-7f45}

Part 2 reuses the project from the Raspberry Pi object detection lab and the [EdgeML Made Easy](https://mjrovai.github.io/EdgeML_Made_Ease_ebook/raspi/object_detection/custom_object_detection.html) chapter, so the two boards can be compared directly.

### Project Goal {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-project-goal-4c4a}

The scenario is an industrial facility that must **sort and count wheels and special boxes** passing in front of a camera.

\noindent
![](images/jpeg/proj_goal.jpg){width=70% fig-align="center"}

Each image may contain any number of boxes and wheels, or none at all:

- **box**
- **wheel**
- (background, meaning no objects, is handled implicitly)

The system should **continuously** capture frames, detect every object, count them by class, and show the counts on the UNO Q's LED matrix:

```text
USB webcam -> VideoObjectDetection Brick -> custom EI model
                                                  |
                                {"Box": [...], "Wheel": [...]}
                                                  |
                                     count per class (Python)
                                                  |
                            Bridge.call("show_counts", boxes, wheels)
                                                  |
                                        MCU (Arduino sketch)
                                        -> LED matrix: boxes | wheels
```

As in the Image Classification lab, the custom model is deployed in two steps:

- **Path A** (@sec-uno-q-object-detection-deploying-uno-q-path-object-detection-brick-2028) uses the **Object Detection Brick**, reusing the static image example with the custom model. It is quick to set up and ideal for checking the model.
- **Path B** (@sec-uno-q-object-detection-deploying-uno-q-path-b-live-camera-5817) uses the **Video Object Detection Brick** for live camera inference, and @sec-uno-q-object-detection-postprocessing-counting-mcu-actuation-via-bridge-d4a5 adds counting and MCU actuation. **This is the path for real projects.**

## Data Collection and Labeling {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-data-collection-labeling-1199}

An object detection dataset needs more than images in labeled folders: every object in every image needs a **bounding box** and a label. That makes labeling the most time-consuming part of the project.

### Option A: Use the Ready-Made Dataset (Recommended for a First Run) {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-option-use-readymade-dataset-recommended-first-run-8c8c}

The labeled, preprocessed dataset from the Raspberry Pi project is public on Roboflow Universe: [box-versus-wheel-auto-dataset](https://universe.roboflow.com/marcelo-rovai-riila/box-versus-wheel-auto-dataset). It has **153 images at 320×320**, already split into train, validation, and test sets, with augmentation applied.

Download it in **YOLOv8** format (a zip file). Inside, each split has an `images` folder and a `labels` folder. Every `image_id.jpg` has a matching `image_id.txt` with one line per object, `class_id x_center y_center width height`, normalized to the image size. `data.yaml` maps the class IDs to names: `0` is `box` and `1` is `wheel` (alphabetical order).

\noindent
![](images/jpeg/dataset-struct.jpg){width=70% fig-align="center"}

### Option B: Capture and Label New Images {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-option-b-capture-label-new-images-d266}

A model trained on the actual objects, under the actual lighting, performs better on the actual bench. To capture on the UNO Q, reuse the `capture_images.py` script from the [Image Classification](../image_classification/image_classification.qmd#sec-uno-q-image-classification-option-b-capturing-images-uno-q-09dc) lab, with two changes: set `label = "box-wheel"` (the real labels are added later, per object), and capture at **320×320** or crop to square afterward.

> Capture about 60 images. Vary the angles, backgrounds, distances, and lighting, and vary **how many** objects appear in each frame, from zero to several of each kind. Include some frames with **no objects at all**.

Copy the images to the host computer (`scp -r arduino@<UNO_Q_IP>:~/dataset ./dataset`) and label them. Labeling works directly in Edge Impulse Studio (**Data acquisition > Labeling queue**), or in [Roboflow](https://roboflow.com), as in the Raspberry Pi project, which offers auto-labeling and exports to several formats:

1. Create a project (for example, "box-versus-wheel") and upload the raw images.
2. Draw a box around every object, or use **Auto Label** / **Label Assist** and correct its suggestions.

\noindent
![](images/jpeg/annotation.jpg){width=85% fig-align="center"}

3. Mark background-only images with the **Null** tool, so they are kept with no annotations.

\noindent
![](images/png/null-tool.png){width=70% fig-align="center"}

4. Split into train, validation, and test, resize to **320×320** (stretch), and add augmentation (for example, ±15° rotation, crop, brightness, and exposure).

\noindent
![](images/png/pre-proc.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

5. Export in **YOLOv8** format.

> **Why not label in Edge Impulse directly?** For a small dataset, it is the shortest path. A dataset labeled on a free Edge Impulse account cannot be exported for training elsewhere, though, while a Roboflow export can also train a YOLO model with Ultralytics, as in the Raspberry Pi lab.

### Upload to Edge Impulse Studio {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-upload-edge-impulse-studio-116d}

1. In Edge Impulse Studio, create a new project (for example, "UNO-Q - Custom Object Detection").
2. On the **Dashboard**, under **Project info**, set the **Labeling method** to **Bounding boxes (object detection)**.
3. Go to **Data acquisition > Upload data**. Choose **Select a folder**, pick the `train` folder (with its `images` and `labels` subfolders), set the label format to **YOLO TXT**, choose the **Training** category, and upload.
4. Repeat for the `test` and `valid` folders, into the **Test** category.

\noindent
![](images/png/upload-data.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

> **Check the label names.** After uploading, open a few samples. If the objects are labeled `0` and `1` instead of `box` and `wheel`, the class names did not come across. Rename them now (in **Data acquisition**, filter by label and use **Edit labels**), because these strings are exactly what the Python callbacks match against later.

\noindent
![](images/png/ei-data.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

> **Shortcut:** the project used in this lab is public: [UNO Q - Custom Object Detection](https://studio.edgeimpulse.com/public/894640/live). Click **Clone** to copy it, dataset and impulses included, and compare the results.

## Training the Models with Edge Impulse Studio {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-training-models-edge-impulse-studio-38cd}

This lab trains **two** models on the same dataset and compares them on the board: **FOMO**, the fastest option, and **YOLO**, the most precise. Edge Impulse's **Experiments** feature lets one project hold both impulses side by side.

### How FOMO Works {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-fomo-works-9cea}

FOMO (Faster Objects, More Objects) uses a **MobileNetV2** backbone to extract a feature map, then classifies each cell of a coarse grid instead of regressing box coordinates. The image is divided by a factor of 8, so a 160×160 input becomes a 20×20 grid, and each cell answers "is the center of a box, or of a wheel, here?"

\noindent
![](images/jpeg/fomo-1.jpg){width=85% fig-align="center"}

Neighboring cells that fire for the same class are merged into one object, located at their **centroid**.

\noindent
![](images/png/fomo-works.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

The trade-off is clear:

- **What FOMO gains**: speed and memory. The FOMO model itself is much smaller and faster than SSD or YOLO, and it handles many small, well-separated objects well. (In an application, the end-to-end gap is smaller than the models alone suggest, as @sec-uno-q-object-detection-deploying-uno-q-path-object-detection-brick-2028 measures.)
- **What FOMO loses**: object size. FOMO reports where an object is, not how big it is. The "box" it returns is a cell-sized square around the centroid, not a fitted rectangle. The Brick's `draw_bounding_boxes()` knows this: for a FOMO model, it draws **circles** instead of rectangles.

For counting boxes and wheels, size does not matter, so FOMO is a good fit. Anything that needs an object's extent (distance estimation, cropping an object for a second model, overlap checks) needs YOLO.

### Impulse 1: FOMO {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-impulse-1-fomo-1a72}

1. Go to **Create impulse**. When asked for a target device, choose **Arduino UNO Q** (this only affects the latency estimates, not the training).
2. Set the input to **160×160**, resize mode **Squash**.
3. Add an **Image** processing block and an **Object Detection (Images)** learning block.
4. Click **Save Impulse**.
5. In the **Image** tab, set **Color depth** to **RGB**, then click **Save parameters** and **Generate features**.
6. In the **Object detection** tab, choose **FOMO (Faster Objects, More Objects) MobileNetV2 0.35**.
7. Train with **60 epochs**, learning rate **0.001**, and **no data augmentation** if the dataset is the Roboflow one, which is already augmented.

Edge Impulse reports an **F1 score** for FOMO rather than mAP, because there are no boxes to compute IoU against, only centroids.

\noindent
![](images/png/fi-fomo.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

> For FOMO, this lab uses the **float32** version. The model is small in memory and fast, and in training the quantized (int8) version's F1 score dropped below 0.70.

### Impulse 2: YOLO {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-impulse-2-yolo-6512}

1. Go to **Experiments** and create a new impulse.
2. Set the input to **320×320** (the resolution of the Roboflow dataset).
3. Add **Image** and **Object Detection (Images)** blocks and generate RGB features as before.
4. In the **Object detection** tab, choose a **YOLO** architecture. At the time of writing, Edge Impulse offers its own **YOLO-Pro** family. Start with the Small variant (6.9M parameters).
5. Train, starting with **30 epochs** (YOLO benefits from more, given the time).

Edge Impulse reports **mAP@0.5** (and mAP@[0.5:0.95]) for this model.

> For YOLO-Pro Small, this lab deploys the **quantized (int8)** version. Check its mAP in the **Model version** selector before deploying: if it is close to the float32 value, int8 is the better choice, because it is smaller and usually faster on the UNO Q's CPU.

\noindent
![](images/png/yolo-train.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

### Test Both Models {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-test-both-models-6a73}

Go to **Model testing**, select the version to deploy (float32 for FOMO, int8 for YOLO), and click **Classify all** for each impulse. Look at the test images where the models disagree: FOMO typically misses objects that touch each other (their centroids fall in the same cell), while YOLO is more likely than expected to miss very small objects at 320×320.

Record the results for comparison with the on-board measurements in @sec-uno-q-object-detection-performance-analysis-3b31.

+-----------------------+-------------+-----------------------+----------------------------+
| **Model**             | **Input**   | **Metric (test set)** | **Estimated latency (EI)** |
+:======================+:============+:======================+:===========================+
| FOMO MobileNetV2 0.35 | 160×160     | F1 = **0.82**         | **11** ms                  |
+-----------------------+-------------+-----------------------+----------------------------+
| YOLO-Pro Small (6.9M) | 320×320     | mAP@0.5 = **0.99**    | **1,841** ms               |
+-----------------------+-------------+-----------------------+----------------------------+

: Test-set results and Edge Impulse latency estimates. {#tbl-uno-q-object-detection-ei-results}

> **F1 and mAP are not directly comparable.** FOMO's F1 counts a detection as correct when its centroid lands on the right object; YOLO's mAP@0.5 also requires the predicted box to overlap the labeled box by at least 50%. So 0.82 against 0.99 does not mean YOLO is "20% better". Compare the models on what the application needs, here whether the counts are right, and on latency.

> **A smaller YOLO is also an option.** The smallest variant, YOLO-Pro Pico (682K parameters), would have a much lower latency, probably at the cost of some mAP. When boxes are needed rather than centroids but YOLO-Pro Small turns out too slow, train a smaller variant as a third experiment and compare. YOLO-Pro Nano (2.4M parameters, int8) kept mAP@0.5 at 0.99 on the validation set, counted all six test images correctly, and ran more than twice as fast as Small on the live stream (see @sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-7-try-smaller-yolo-30a8 and @sec-uno-q-object-detection-performance-analysis-3b31). As the next section shows, measure on the board before deciding: the Edge Impulse estimate above turned out far too pessimistic.

## Deploying to the UNO Q, Path A: Object Detection Brick {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-deploying-uno-q-path-object-detection-brick-2028}

This path puts the custom model into the static image example from Part 1. It is limited to uploads, but it is the fastest way to see the model running on the board and to inspect what it returns.

### Step 1: Copy the Pre-Installed Example {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-1-copy-preinstalled-example-854c}

```bash
cp -r /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
object-detection/ ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks
```

The copy appears in App Lab's **Apps** list, but still as **Detect objects on images**: App Lab shows the `name:` field from `app.yaml`, not the folder name, and `cp` copied the example's `app.yaml` unchanged. Give it its own name:

```bash
sed -i 's/^name: .*/name: My Detector (Custom Images)/' \
  ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks/app.yaml
```

Alternatively, in Arduino App Lab, copy **Detect objects on images** to **My Apps** under a new name, which sets the name automatically.

\noindent
![](images/png/app-lab-mydetector.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

### Step 2: Export the Model from Edge Impulse to Arduino App Lab {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-2-export-model-edge-impulse-arduino-app-lab-577e}

This is the same flow as in the [Image Classification](../image_classification/image_classification.qmd#sec-uno-q-image-classification-step-2-export-model-edge-impulse-arduino-app-lab-c482) lab:

1. In the copied app, open **Bricks > Object Detection > AI models** and click **Train new AI model**.
2. Log in to the Arduino / Edge Impulse account and open the object detection project.
3. Make sure the impulse to deploy (start with **FOMO**) is the active one.
4. In **Deployment**, select **Arduino UNO Q** as the target. Under model optimizations, choose the same version tested earlier (**float32**, unoptimized), and click **Build**.
5. When the build finishes, click **Go to Arduino** to send the model to App Lab.

\noindent
![](images/png/fomo-custom.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

### Step 3: Select the Model on the UNO Q {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-3-select-model-uno-q-1ed9}

In the app's **AI Models** area, download the model to the UNO Q and select it. `app.yaml` is updated to point to it:

```yaml
name: My Detector (Custom Images)
icon: 🏞️
description: Custom object detection in the browser
bricks:
- arduino:web_ui: {}
- arduino:object_detection:
    model: ei-model-<PROJECT_ID>-1
```

App Lab stores the model in its own folder, `/home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/models/custom-ei/ei-model-<PROJECT_ID>-<VERSION>/`.

### Alternative to Steps 2 and 3: Load the `.eim` File Directly {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-alternative-steps-2-3-load-eim-file-directly-8d8a}

The App Lab flow above works, but it takes several hops between Edge Impulse, App Lab, and the board. There is a shorter path: download the model file and point the Brick at it.

It works because of how the Brick runs the model. The Object Detection Brick starts the Edge Impulse runner in a container with `--model-file ${EI_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL}`, and that container can see the folder `/home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/ei-models`. Any variable set in a Brick's `variables:` block in `app.yaml` is passed to the container and takes priority over the default model.

1. In Edge Impulse **Deployment**, select **Arduino UNO Q** (or **Linux (AARCH64)**), choose **float32**, and click **Build**. The browser downloads a file such as `uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v12-fomo-mobilenetv2.eim`.

2. Copy it to the board (from the host computer):

```bash
scp ~/Downloads/uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v12-\
fomo-mobilenetv2.eim arduino@<UNO_Q_IP>:~/
```

3. On the UNO Q, move it into the models folder under a short name, and make it executable (an `.eim` file is a program, and the runner needs to execute it):

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models
mv ~/uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v12-fomo-mobilenetv2.eim \
  ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-fomo.eim
chmod +x ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-fomo.eim
```

4. Edit `app.yaml`: **remove the `model:` line** and set the variable instead. Removing `model:` is not optional. When it is present, the CLI applies that model's configuration, which mounts only the App Lab model's own folder into the container, so the runner cannot see `ei-models/` and fails with `ENOENT: no such file or directory`. Selecting a model in App Lab writes the line back, so check `app.yaml` again after going back to App Lab.

   Any terminal editor works. With `nano app.yaml`, place the cursor on a line and press **Ctrl+K** to delete it, then type the new lines and save with **Ctrl+O**, **Enter**, **Ctrl+X**. The result:

```yaml
name: My Detector (Custom Images)
icon: 🏞️
description: Custom object detection in the browser
bricks:
- arduino:web_ui: {}
- arduino:object_detection:
    variables:
      EI_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL: >-
        /home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-fomo.eim
```

5. Start the app:

```bash
cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks
arduino-app-cli app start .
```

\noindent
![](images/png/eim-direct-start.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

Upload an image in the browser: if the labels are **Box** and **Wheel**, the Brick is running the custom model. COCO classes such as *cup* or *person* mean the variable did not take effect; check the path and the `chmod`. If the app fails to start with `container ... ei-obj-detection-runner-1 is unhealthy`, read the runner's own log, which shows the actual error:

```bash
docker logs --tail 20 my-detector-bricks-ei-obj-detection-runner-1
```

This option has a second advantage: switching models becomes a one-line change. Copy the YOLO `.eim` next to the FOMO one, and the two can be compared by editing `app.yaml` and restarting the app.

### Step 4: Print Model Info, Detections, and Latency {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-4-print-model-info-detections-latency-d163}

Before running, replace `python/main.py` with a version that also prints what the model expects and what it finds. The model info is worth reading once: it gives the **exact label strings** the callbacks must use, the input size, and the model type (`object_detection` for YOLO, `constrained_object_detection` for FOMO).

```python
from arduino.app_utils import App
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.object_detection import ObjectDetection
from PIL import Image
import io
import base64
import time

object_detection = ObjectDetection()


def print_model_info(detector):
    info = detector.get_model_info()
    if info is None:
        print("Failed to retrieve model info.")
        return
    print("Model info:")
    for attr in dir(info):
        if not attr.startswith("_") and not callable(getattr(info, attr)):
            print(f"  {attr}: {getattr(info, attr)}")


def encode_png(pil_image):
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    pil_image.save(buf, format="PNG")
    return base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode("utf-8")


def on_detect_objects(client_id, data):
    try:
        image_data = data.get("image")
        confidence = data.get("confidence", 0.5)
        if not image_data:
            ui.send_message("detection_error",
                            {"error": "No image data"})
            return

        pil_image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(base64.b64decode(image_data)))

        start = time.perf_counter()
        results = object_detection.detect(pil_image,
                                          confidence=confidence)
        latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000

        if results is None:
            ui.send_message("detection_error",
                            {"error": "No results returned"})
            return

        detections = results.get("detection", [])
        counts = {}
        for obj in detections:
            name = obj["class_name"]
            counts[name] = counts.get(name, 0) + 1
            box = [round(v) for v in obj["bounding_box_xyxy"]]
            print(f"  {name:6s} {float(obj['confidence']):5.1f}%  "
                  f"box={box}")
        print(f"Counts: {counts}  |  Latency: {latency_ms:.1f} ms\n",
              flush=True)

        annotated = object_detection.draw_bounding_boxes(pil_image,
                                                         results)
        if annotated is None:
            annotated = pil_image
        ui.send_message("detection_result", {
            "success": True,
            "result_image": encode_png(annotated),
            "detection_count": len(detections),
            "processing_time": f"{latency_ms:.2f} ms",
        })

    except Exception as e:
        ui.send_message("detection_error", {"error": str(e)})


print_model_info(object_detection)
ui = WebUI()
ui.on_message("detect_objects", on_detect_objects)

App.run()
```

### Step 5: Run the App {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-5-run-app-5964}

```bash
cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks
arduino-app-cli app start .
```

In a second terminal, follow the logs:

```bash
cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks
arduino-app-cli app logs . --follow
```

Open `http://<UNO_Q_IP>:7000` and upload test images of boxes and wheels (the `test` folder of the dataset is a good source). For the FOMO model, the browser shows **circles** at each object's centroid. The log shows each detection, the counts, and the latency.

\noindent
![](images/png/custom-objdet-result.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

Here the FOMO model got everything right: three boxes and one wheel, each marked by a circle at its centroid. Note the labels, **Box** and **Wheel**, with capital letters: these are the exact strings the code must match in @sec-uno-q-object-detection-postprocessing-counting-mcu-actuation-via-bridge-d4a5.

More test images, though, quickly show FOMO's limits. Two failures are typical:

- **Missed objects.** In the image below, the model found three of the four wheels and one of the three boxes. The misses are objects cut by the image edge, partly hidden behind others, or seen from an unusual angle.

\noindent
![](images/png/fomo-misses.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

- **One object, several centroids.** When an object is large in the frame, it covers many cells of FOMO's grid, and separate groups of cells can each report a centroid. The single box below was counted three times.

\noindent
![](images/png/fomo-split.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

Both explain why the F1 score in @tbl-uno-q-object-detection-ei-results was 0.82, and both matter for counting: a miss lowers the count, a split raises it. Keep the objects at roughly the distance and size they had in the training images, and if they must appear large in the frame, prefer YOLO, which fits one box to each object.

The log for six test images, starting with the one above:

\noindent
![](images/png/infer-fomo-log.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

Three things are worth reading in it:

- **The model info** confirms what was trained: a 160×160 input, two labels, `['Box', 'Wheel']`, and `model_type: constrained_object_detection`, which is how Edge Impulse identifies a FOMO model (a YOLO model reports `object_detection`).
- **The boxes are small, fixed-size squares** (16 or 32 pixels wide), centered on each object, because FOMO reports centroids, not object sizes. Their coordinates also go up to 288, beyond the model's 160×160 input: the Brick returns them **in the uploaded image's pixel space**, so they can be used directly on the original image.
- **The first inference is the slowest.** The first and third images are the same file, with identical detections, yet they took 232.6 ms and 159.4 ms. The first call after the app starts pays a one-time warm-up cost. Ignoring it, the other five took between 146 and 186 ms, about **160 ms** on average, against an estimate of about 11 ms in Edge Impulse.

> **Latency here includes more than the model.** The time measured around `detect()` also covers encoding the image, sending it to the model runner container over HTTP, resizing it to 160×160, and returning the result. The model itself is a small fraction of the 160 ms. When measuring, always discard the first call and average several. That end-to-end number is the one the application actually sees, and it is why Edge Impulse's estimate alone is not enough to choose a model.

### Step 6: Repeat with YOLO {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-6-repeat-yolo-337a}

Deploy the **YOLO-Pro Small** impulse the same way, this time choosing **Quantized (int8)** under model optimizations. With the direct `.eim` option, this is a one-line change in `app.yaml` (point `EI_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL` to `box-wheel-yolo.eim`) and an app restart. Copy and rename the file as for FOMO:

```bash
mv ~/uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v15-yolo-pro-small.eim \
  ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo.eim
chmod +x ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo.eim
```

Upload the same test images.

The browser now shows fitted **rectangles**, and the two scenes where FOMO failed come out right. The single large box is counted once:

\noindent
![](images/png/yolo-single-box.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

And the crowded scene, where FOMO found three wheels and one box, is now complete, with four wheels and three boxes:

\noindent
![](images/png/yolo-many-objects.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

YOLO counted all six test images correctly, against two for FOMO. The log shows why it costs more:

\noindent
![](images/png/inference-yolo.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

- **The model info** reports a 320×320 input and `model_type: object_detection`, the YOLO family. The labels are the same, so the Python code does not change.
- **The boxes now have real sizes**, fitted to each object.
- **The latency is about 331 ms** on average after the warm-up call (536 ms), about twice FOMO's 160 ms.

That last number deserves a second look. Edge Impulse estimated **1,841 ms** for this model, more than five times what the board actually measured. For FOMO, the estimate was 11 ms against 160 ms measured. The estimates were wrong in both directions: one ignores the fixed cost of moving the image to the runner, and the other did not anticipate how fast the runner executes this model on the UNO Q. **Always measure on the board before choosing a model.**

### Step 7: Try a Smaller YOLO {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-7-try-smaller-yolo-30a8}

If YOLO-Pro Small counts well but more speed is needed, train a smaller variant and compare it on the board. Here, **YOLO-Pro Nano** (2.4M parameters) was trained, deployed as **Quantized (int8)**, and installed next to the others:

```bash
mv ~/uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v16-yolo-pro-nano.eim \
  ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo-nano.eim
chmod +x ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo-nano.eim
```

With `EI_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL` pointed to `box-wheel-yolo-nano.eim` and the app restarted, it also counted all six test images correctly, including the crowded scene:

\noindent
![](images/png/yolo-nano-result.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

In the timing script of @sec-uno-q-object-detection-performance-analysis-3b31, it took about 221 ms per image, against 342 ms for Small in the same measurement. @tbl-uno-q-object-detection-latency compares all the models side by side.

## Deploying to the UNO Q, Path B: Live Camera {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-deploying-uno-q-path-b-live-camera-5817}

Path B moves to the live camera. Rather than building a web page from scratch, it starts from the **Detect Objects on Camera** example, which already streams the annotated video to the browser, and swaps in the custom model.

### Step 1: Copy the Live Camera Example {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-1-copy-live-camera-example-d623}

```bash
cp -r /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
video-generic-object-detection/ ~/ArduinoApps/box-wheel-counter
sed -i 's/^name: .*/name: Box Wheel Counter/' \
  ~/ArduinoApps/box-wheel-counter/app.yaml
```

As in Path A, the `sed` line renames the app in App Lab's list. Alternatively, copy **Detect Objects on Camera** to **My Apps** in App Lab, naming it `Box Wheel Counter`.

### Step 2: Select the Model {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-2-select-model-a35e}

From here on, the lab uses **YOLO-Pro Nano**, which counted every test image correctly in Path A and is the fastest of the YOLO models. (YOLO-Pro Small and FOMO work too, with the same code; only the model file changes.)

Open **Bricks > Video Object Detection > AI Models** and select the YOLO-Pro Nano model deployed in Path A (the same `.eim` works with both Bricks). `app.yaml` becomes:

```yaml
name: Box Wheel Counter
icon: 📽️
description: Count boxes and wheels on a live camera feed
bricks:
- arduino:video_object_detection:
    model: ei-model-<PROJECT_ID>-1
- arduino:web_ui: {}
```

If the `.eim` file was loaded directly in Path A, do the same here. The video Brick uses a different variable name, `EI_V_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL`, and, as in Path A, there is no `model:` line. The complete `app.yaml` is:

```yaml
name: Box Wheel Counter
icon: 📽️
description: Count boxes and wheels on a live camera feed
bricks:
- arduino:video_object_detection:
    variables:
      EI_V_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL: >-
        /home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo-nano.eim
- arduino:web_ui: {}
```

Edit it with `nano app.yaml`, as in Path A (**Ctrl+K** deletes the `model:` line).

### Step 3: Run It Unchanged {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-3-run-unchanged-ce5f}

The example's `main.py` is generic: it forwards every detection to the browser, whatever the labels are. So the app already works with the custom model, without changing a line of Python.

```bash
cd ~/ArduinoApps/box-wheel-counter
arduino-app-cli app start .
```

Open `http://<UNO_Q_IP>:7000`, place boxes and wheels in front of the camera, and watch the detections appear on the video and in the list. Use the slider to find the threshold where real objects are detected reliably and empty background produces nothing.

\noindent
![](images/png/live-custom-objdet.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

This screenshot was taken with YOLO-Pro Small, before the switch to Nano. With the threshold at 0.76, the model finds the two boxes and the wheel, each with a tight bounding box at about 0.91 confidence. The **Box** and **Wheel** labels confirm that the video Brick is running the custom `.eim` file: `EI_V_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL` took effect, even though it is not among the Brick's declared variables.

> The web page's "special reactions" are keyed to COCO classes (cat, cup, and so on), so they never fire for `box` or `wheel`. That is expected.

### Step 4: The `VideoObjectDetection` Class {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-4-videoobjectdetection-class-56fd}

Before modifying the code, here is what the Brick offers:

```python
class VideoObjectDetection(camera: BaseCamera | None = None,
                           confidence: float = 0.3,
                           debounce_sec: float = 0.0,
                           camera_preview: bool = False)
```

- **camera**: the camera to use. If `None`, the default USB camera is opened.
- **confidence**: the minimum confidence (0.0 to 1.0) for a detection to reach the callbacks.
- **debounce_sec**: the minimum time between two triggers **for the same label**. Useful for alarms ("a wheel appeared"), harmful for counting, which needs every frame. This lab keeps it at 0.
- **camera_preview**: if `True`, a callback that declares a `frame` parameter also receives the current camera frame as JPEG bytes, without boxes drawn. Useful for saving snapshots of detections.

There are two ways to receive detections:

- `on_detect("wheel", callback)`: called whenever a specific label appears. The callback can take no arguments, or one dict with `confidence` and `bounding_box_xyxy`. If a frame has three wheels, it is called three times.
- `on_detect_all(callback)`: called **once per frame** with all detections, grouped by label. This is the one for counting.

One behavior is not obvious from the API, and it matters for this project: **neither callback is called when a frame has no detections.** When the last box leaves the camera's view, the code receives nothing at all. It does not receive "zero boxes"; it simply stops hearing from the Brick. The next section deals with that.

## Post-Processing: Counting and MCU Actuation via Bridge {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-postprocessing-counting-mcu-actuation-via-bridge-d4a5}

Live detection now runs. This section turns the detections into **counts per class** and sends them to the MCU, which shows them on the LED matrix: **boxes on the left half, wheels on the right**, one 2×2 block per object.

### Architecture {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-bridge-architecture-d03f}

```text
USB webcam -> VideoObjectDetection Brick -> on_detect_all(detections)
                                                    |
                                     counts = (len(box), len(wheel))
                                     stamped with the time of the frame
                                                    |
                    user_loop (every 100 ms): no frame for 1 s -> (0, 0)
                                                    |  (only on change)
                                  Bridge.call("show_counts", boxes, wheels)
                                                    |
                                          MCU (Arduino sketch)
                                          -> LED matrix:  ■ ■ ■ | ■ ■ ■
                                                          boxes | wheels
```

Two design decisions are worth explaining:

- **The callback does not call the Bridge.** `on_detect_all` runs on a pool of worker threads, several frames per second. If it called the MCU directly, calls could overlap and arrive out of order. Instead, the callback only **records** the latest counts, under a lock. A single `user_loop` reads them and is the only code that talks to the MCU.
- **"Nothing seen" is a timeout.** Since the Brick is silent when a frame is empty, the loop treats "no detections for 1 second" as "zero objects". Without this, the matrix would freeze on the last count forever after the objects were removed. This is the most common bug in live detection apps, and it is easy to miss in testing, because testing usually means putting objects *in front of* the camera.

> **Match the timeout to the model.** The timeout must be longer than the time between two frames, or the count drops to zero between every pair of frames and the matrix blinks. A good rule is about three times the time between frames. Live, the models here deliver a new frame every 100 ms (FOMO), 130 ms (YOLO-Pro Nano), or 300 ms (YOLO-Pro Small), as @sec-uno-q-object-detection-performance-analysis-3b31 shows, so one second covers all of them. For a slower live stream, for example with a larger model, raise `EMPTY_AFTER_SEC` accordingly.

### Step 1: Add a Sketch to the Project {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-1-add-sketch-project-66ef}

```bash
cd ~/ArduinoApps/box-wheel-counter
mkdir -p sketch
```

### Step 2: Write the Arduino Sketch {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-2-write-arduino-sketch-95ef}

Create `sketch/sketch.ino`:

```cpp
#include "Arduino_RouterBridge.h"
#include "Arduino_LED_Matrix.h"

ArduinoLEDMatrix matrix;

// 8 rows x 13 columns, 0 = off, 1 = on.
// Row 0 is the top row, column 0 is the left column.
uint8_t frame[8][13];

const int MAX_PER_SIDE   = 12;  // 3 blocks across x 4 blocks down
const int DIVIDER_COL    = 6;
const int BOX_BASE_COL   = 0;   // columns 0..5
const int WHEEL_BASE_COL = 7;   // columns 7..12

// Light a 2x2 block for the k-th object (k = 0..11) on one side.
void drawBlock(int k, int baseCol) {
  int row = (k / 3) * 2;
  int col = baseCol + (k % 3) * 2;
  frame[row][col]         = 1;
  frame[row][col + 1]     = 1;
  frame[row + 1][col]     = 1;
  frame[row + 1][col + 1] = 1;
}

void show_counts(int boxes, int wheels) {
  memset(frame, 0, sizeof(frame));

  // The divider is always on, to show the app is alive
  for (int r = 0; r < 8; r++) frame[r][DIVIDER_COL] = 1;

  boxes  = constrain(boxes,  0, MAX_PER_SIDE);
  wheels = constrain(wheels, 0, MAX_PER_SIDE);
  for (int k = 0; k < boxes;  k++) drawBlock(k, BOX_BASE_COL);
  for (int k = 0; k < wheels; k++) drawBlock(k, WHEEL_BASE_COL);

  matrix.renderBitmap(frame, 8, 13);
}

void setup() {
  matrix.begin();
  show_counts(0, 0);

  Bridge.begin();
  // provide_safe runs the handler in the loop() context, where
  // hardware calls such as renderBitmap are safe.
  Bridge.provide_safe("show_counts", show_counts);
}

void loop() {
  // All work is event-driven via Bridge calls from Python.
}
```

Create `sketch/sketch.yaml`:

```yaml
profiles:
  default:
    fqbn: arduino:zephyr:uno_q
    platforms:
      - platform: arduino:zephyr
    libraries:
      - dependency: Arduino_RPClite (0.2.1)
default_profile: default
```

> `Arduino_LED_Matrix` is bundled with the `arduino:zephyr` core and needs no `libraries:` entry. If the left and right halves appear swapped or upside down on the board, it is an orientation issue: mirror the row or column index in `drawBlock()` to match the board.

### Step 3: Update the Python Script {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-3-update-python-script-a70c}

Replace `python/main.py`. It keeps the browser features of the original example (the live detection list and the threshold slider) and adds counting and the Bridge:

```python
import threading
import time
from datetime import datetime, UTC

from arduino.app_utils import App, Bridge
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.video_objectdetection import (
    VideoObjectDetection,
)

# Labels exactly as the model reports them (check "labels" in the
# model info printed in Path A; if they are "0" and "1", use those).
BOX_LABEL = "Box"
WHEEL_LABEL = "Wheel"

CONFIDENCE = 0.5
# No detections for this long -> counts are zero (about 3x the time
# between frames; 1.0 covers FOMO and both YOLO-Pro models)
EMPTY_AFTER_SEC = 1.0
LOOP_PERIOD_SEC = 0.1

ui = WebUI()
detection_stream = VideoObjectDetection(confidence=CONFIDENCE,
                                        debounce_sec=0.0)

ui.on_message(
    "override_th",
    lambda sid, threshold: detection_stream.override_threshold(threshold),
)

# Shared between the detection callback (worker threads) and user_loop
state_lock = threading.Lock()
latest_counts = (0, 0)
last_detection_time = 0.0

shown_counts = None  # what the MCU currently displays (user_loop only)


def on_all_detections(detections: dict):
    """Called once per frame that has at least one detection."""
    global latest_counts, last_detection_time

    counts = (len(detections.get(BOX_LABEL, [])),
              len(detections.get(WHEEL_LABEL, [])))
    with state_lock:
        latest_counts = counts
        last_detection_time = time.monotonic()

    # Keep the original example's live list in the browser
    for label, values in detections.items():
        for value in values:
            ui.send_message("detection", message={
                "content": label,
                "confidence": value.get("confidence"),
                "timestamp": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(),
            })


detection_stream.on_detect_all(on_all_detections)


def loop():
    """The only place that talks to the MCU."""
    global shown_counts

    with state_lock:
        if time.monotonic() - last_detection_time > EMPTY_AFTER_SEC:
            counts = (0, 0)  # the Brick is silent on empty frames
        else:
            counts = latest_counts

    if counts != shown_counts:
        try:
            Bridge.call("show_counts", counts[0], counts[1])
            shown_counts = counts
            print(f"==> boxes: {counts[0]}  wheels: {counts[1]}",
                  flush=True)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Bridge call failed: {e}", flush=True)

    time.sleep(LOOP_PERIOD_SEC)


App.run(user_loop=loop)
```

A few details:

- `shown_counts` starts as `None`, so the first pass of the loop always sends the counts, even if they are `(0, 0)`. That resynchronizes the matrix if the Python side restarts while the sketch keeps running.
- `shown_counts` is updated only **after** a successful call. If the MCU is momentarily unreachable, the loop tries again on the next pass.
- `App.run(user_loop=loop)` calls `loop()` repeatedly. The Bridge is up by the time `loop()` first runs, which is why the Bridge call lives there and not above `App.run()`.

### Step 6: Test the System {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-step-6-test-system-330a}

Follow the logs:

```bash

```

Then work through these cases, in this order:

1. **One box** in view: one block lights on the left, and the log shows `boxes: 1  wheels: 0`.
2. **Add two wheels**: two blocks light on the right.
3. **Remove everything**: after about one second, the matrix returns to just the divider. If it does not, the empty-frame timeout is not working.
4. **Hold an object at the edge of the frame**, or tilt it until it is half hidden: the count may flicker between two values. That is the threshold and the model's uncertainty showing through, which Exercise 3 addresses.

### Extending the MCU Actuation {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-extending-mcu-actuation-0c42}

Because the MCU now receives numbers rather than a label, the sketch can react to quantities.

**Alarm when a batch is complete:**

```cpp
#define BUZZER_PIN 3
const int BATCH_SIZE = 4;

void show_counts(int boxes, int wheels) {
  // ... matrix drawing as before ...
  if (wheels >= BATCH_SIZE) tone(BUZZER_PIN, 2000, 200);
}
```

**Sort with a servo**, steering toward whichever class is in the majority:

```cpp
#include <Servo.h>
Servo gate;   // call gate.attach(pin) in setup()

void show_counts(int boxes, int wheels) {
  // ... matrix drawing as before ...
  if (boxes > wheels)      gate.write(0);
  else if (wheels > boxes) gate.write(180);
  else                     gate.write(90);
}
```

## Performance Analysis {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-performance-analysis-3b31}

### Inference Latency {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-inference-latency-b7bb}

All the models were measured on the same UNO Q (4 GB) in two ways:

- **Path A (per image):** a small app called `ObjectDetection.detect()` on six 320×320 images from the dataset, five rounds after one warm-up call, timing each call in Python. This is the end-to-end time the code waits, including the transfer to the model runner.
- **Path B (live stream):** with the Video Object Detection Brick running, a script counted the result messages that the model runner sends for each camera frame over 30 seconds.

+----------------------------+-------------+---------------------+-------------+------------------+--------------------+
| **Model**                  | **Input**   | **Path A latency**  | **Warm-up** | **Path B live**  | **Test metric**    |
|                            |             | **(mean of 30)**    | **call**    | **FPS**          |                    |
+:===========================+:============+====================:+============:+:=================+:===================+
| FOMO MobileNetV2 0.35      | 160×160     | 139 ms              | 260 ms      | ~10 FPS (camera  | F1 = 0.82          |
| (float32)                  |             |                     |             | limit)           |                    |
+----------------------------+-------------+---------------------+-------------+------------------+--------------------+
| YOLO-Pro Small (6.9M,      | 320×320     | 342 ms              | 612 ms      | 3.3 FPS          | mAP@0.5 = 0.99     |
| int8)                      |             |                     |             |                  |                    |
+----------------------------+-------------+---------------------+-------------+------------------+--------------------+
| YOLO-Pro Nano (2.4M, int8) | 320×320     | 221 ms              | 454 ms      | ~7.6 FPS         | mAP@0.5 = 0.99     |
+----------------------------+-------------+---------------------+-------------+------------------+--------------------+
| YOLOX-Nano (pre-installed, | 416×416     | 534 ms              | 786 ms      | 1.7 FPS          | n/a                |
| COCO)                      |             |                     |             |                  |                    |
+----------------------------+-------------+---------------------+-------------+------------------+--------------------+

: Latency and live frame rate measured on the UNO Q (4 GB). {#tbl-uno-q-object-detection-latency}

These numbers come from a separate timing run, so they differ a little from the first Path A test (about 160 ms for FOMO and 331 ms for YOLO-Pro Small, with a different set of images). Expect run-to-run differences of 10 to 15% in end-to-end timing. A few things stand out:

- **FOMO runs faster than the camera.** The Brick asks the camera for 10 FPS (the log says `throttling to requested 10 FPS`), and FOMO keeps up with every frame: the runner reports about 23 ms of processing per frame. The rest of the 139 ms in Path A is the trip from Python to the runner and back, not the model.
- **YOLO-Pro Small gives about 3 counts per second**, enough for objects sitting on a bench, and is faster than the pre-installed YOLOX-Nano, which has a larger input and 80 classes.
- **YOLO-Pro Nano more than doubles the live frame rate of Small** (about 7.6 against 3.3 FPS) with the same validation mAP@0.5. In Path A the gain looks smaller (221 against 342 ms), because about 115 ms of every call is the fixed trip to the runner, the same for every model.
- **The first call is always slower.** Ignore it when measuring.

To measure the live frame rate, start the video app and run this script inside its container. It opens a second connection to the runner and counts results for 30 seconds:

```python
# fps.py: run with
#   docker exec -i <app>-main-1 python - < fps.py
import json, time
from websockets.sync.client import connect

with connect("ws://ei-video-obj-detection-runner:4912") as ws:
    stamps = []
    end = time.monotonic() + 30
    while time.monotonic() < end:
        msg = json.loads(ws.recv(timeout=10))
        if msg.get("type") == "classification":
            stamps.append(time.monotonic())

frames = len(stamps) - 1
print(f"{frames / (stamps[-1] - stamps[0]):.2f} FPS")
```

Unlike the `on_detect_all` callback, which stays silent on empty frames, the runner sends a result for every frame, so the count is correct whether or not objects are in view. (The live measurements above were taken with an empty scene.)

### Choosing Between FOMO and YOLO {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-choosing-fomo-yolo-a902}

+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Aspect**                         | **FOMO**                     | **YOLO-Pro Small**             |
+:===================================+:=============================+:===============================+
| **Output**                         | Centroid (drawn as a circle) | Fitted bounding box            |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Speed: Edge Impulse estimate**   | ~11 ms                       | ~1,841 ms                      |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Speed: measured on the UNO Q     | ~139 ms                      | ~342 ms                        |
| (Path A, end to end)**             |                              |                                |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Live frame rate (Path B)**       | ~10 FPS (camera limit)       | 3.3 FPS                        |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Correct counts (6 test images)** | 2 of 6                       | 6 of 6                         |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Small objects**                  | Good (fine grid)             | Depends on input resolution    |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Touching objects**               | May merge into one           | Separates them better          |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Object size / extent**           | Not available                | Available                      |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Best for**                       | Counting, presence, rough    | Measuring, cropping, overlap,  |
|                                    | position                     | tracking                       |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------+

: FOMO and YOLO compared on the box-and-wheel task. {#tbl-uno-q-object-detection-fomo-vs-yolo}

For this project, the measurements decide it: YOLO-Pro Nano counted every test image correctly and runs at about 7.6 frames per second live, which is why the live counter uses it. YOLO-Pro Small counted just as well, but at 3.3 FPS. FOMO is faster still but miscounted four of six images. FOMO remains the right choice when objects are small and well separated, or when the hardware is much weaker than the UNO Q, as on a microcontroller. A good rule: start with the model the accuracy requirement allows, then check that the latency **measured on the board** fits the application, without relying on the estimate.

### Path A vs. Path B {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-path-vs-path-b-2d04}

+-----------------------+---------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| **Aspect**            | **Path A (Object Detection      | **Path B (Video Object Detection      |
|                       | Brick)**                        | Brick)**                              |
+:======================+:================================+:======================================+
| **Input**             | Static images (browser upload)  | Live webcam (continuous)              |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| **Output to Python**  | Full result dict from           | Callbacks, grouped by label           |
|                       | `detect()`                      |                                       |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| **Confidence format** | String, 0–100 (`"87.50"`)       | Float, 0.0–1.0                        |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| **Annotated image**   | `draw_bounding_boxes()` in      | Rendered by the model runner          |
|                       | Python                          | (port 4912)                           |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| **Empty frames**      | Returns an empty `detection`    | No callback at all                    |
|                       | list                            |                                       |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| **MCU actuation**     | Not included                    | Yes, via Bridge RPC                   |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| **Best for**          | Checking a model, demos         | Real-time applications                |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------+---------------------------------------+

: The two deployment paths compared. {#tbl-uno-q-object-detection-paths}

### Comparison with the Raspberry Pi {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-comparison-raspberry-pi-317a}

The same dataset was trained for the Raspberry Pi in [EdgeML Made Easy](https://mjrovai.github.io/EdgeML_Made_Ease_ebook/). There, an SSD MobileNetV2 (320×320) took roughly 0.5 to 1.3 s per image on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and moving to FOMO cut the latency dramatically. On the UNO Q, at the same 320×320 input, YOLO-Pro Small takes about 0.34 s per image end to end (3.3 FPS live) and YOLO-Pro Nano about 0.22 s (about 7.6 FPS live), and FOMO's own processing takes about 23 ms per frame. The UNO Q pipeline adds the hop to the model runner, so compare **end-to-end** times measured on each board, not Edge Impulse's estimates, before drawing conclusions about the hardware.

## Exercises {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-exercises-07a1}

1. **Train on a custom dataset.** Capture and label about 60 images of objects on a real bench (Option B in @sec-uno-q-object-detection-data-collection-labeling-1199). Train YOLO-Pro Nano on it and compare it with the model trained on the Roboflow dataset. Which one counts better on that bench, and why?

2. **Threshold sweep.** In the live app, try thresholds of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. For each, count false positives (blocks lit with no object) and false negatives (objects not counted) over one minute with a fixed arrangement of objects. Which threshold would you ship?

3. **Stabilize the count.** The count flickers when an object is at the edge of the frame. Modify `main.py` so the MCU shows the **most frequent** count over the last N frames (a mode filter) instead of the latest one. How large must N be before the flicker stops, and how much slower does the display react when an object is added or removed?

4. **Left or right?** Use `bounding_box_xyxy` to decide whether each wheel is on the left or the right half of the image, and show the result on the matrix instead of the class split. Where is "the middle"? In Path A, the static Brick returned coordinates in the uploaded image's pixels, not the model's 160×160. Check which space the video Brick uses before hard-coding a value: print a few boxes while moving an object from one edge of the frame to the other.

5. **Log to CSV.** Log each change in the counts (timestamp, boxes, wheels) to a CSV file on the UNO Q. After 5 minutes of adding and removing objects, plot the counts over time.

6. **Snapshot on detection.** Create the detector with `camera_preview=True` and declare `def on_all_detections(detections, frame)`. Save a JPEG whenever the wheel count reaches 3. These snapshots are also a cheap way to collect new training data from the real deployment.

7. **FOMO vs. YOLO on touching objects.** Place two wheels so that they touch. Compare how both models count them.

## Summary {#sec-uno-q-object-detection-summary-eb4a}

This lab moved from *what* the camera sees to *where*, and *how many*:

1. **Part 1**: the pre-installed YOLOX-Nano detector, first on uploaded images (Object Detection Brick) and then on a live camera feed (Video Object Detection Brick), with the annotated video streamed to the browser.
2. **Path A**: a custom box-and-wheel detector, trained in Edge Impulse as both FOMO and YOLO, checked on static images, with the model info, detections, and latency printed in the log.
3. **Path B**: the same model on the live camera, with detections turned into counts per class and sent over Bridge RPC to the MCU, which displays them on the LED matrix.

Key takeaways:

- **Detection = classification + localization.** It is evaluated with IoU and mAP, not accuracy alone, and the confidence threshold is the main knob that trades false positives for false negatives.
- **FOMO and YOLO answer different questions.** FOMO gives *where*, fast. YOLO adds *how big*, and on the test images it also counted far more reliably, at about 1.6 (Nano) to 2.5 (Small) times FOMO's end-to-end latency. Choose by the information and accuracy the application needs.
- **Measure on the board, not in the estimate.** Edge Impulse's latency estimates missed in both directions (11 ms vs. 160 ms measured for FOMO, 1,841 ms vs. 331 ms for YOLO-Pro Small).
- **The Bricks hide the inference pipeline**, including NMS and drawing, so the engineering moves to what the application does with the detections.
- **Live detection needs an explicit "nothing seen" state.** The Video Object Detection Brick is silent on empty frames; a timeout turns that silence into "zero".
- **Keep hardware calls in one place.** Callbacks record state; a single loop talks to the MCU, and only when something changed.

Detection is also where the vision labs meet the generative ones: a fast detector can find *where* to look, and the model from the [Vision-Language Models](../vlm/vlm.qmd) lab can then describe *what* is there, on a crop instead of the whole frame, at a fraction of the cost. Building that pipeline is a natural next project.
